![](images/cos-full-tag-h.webp){width="411"} ![](images/forrt_logo.png){width="237"}

The Center for Open Science and the Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training are [collaborating for the SMART competition](https://www.cos.io/blog/cos-and-forrt-partner-to-increase-discoverability-and-usability-of-replication-evidence). As a result, FORRT will provide validated training data to competition participants. This report describes the data provided alongside it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Terminology

The relation between an article reporting a replication study and the corresponding original study can be complex. The following terms allow for almost every combination of original and replication studies to be documented in the dataset.

+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Term   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

| Entry  | One entry consists of a pair of studies, one of which self-identifies as a replication of the other, using different data than the original study. The replication study investigates at least one central claim from the original report. Each entry has been coded by two independent FReD Data Curators and validated by either a FReD Data Curator or a member of the FReD Core Team. Two entries may originate from the same study but not from the same sample. |
|        |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|        | One entry consists of at least one row but can consist of hundreds of rows: For example, some entries have multiple pairs of original and replication findings (e.g., for many different sub-groups) or do not have a 1:1 correspondence between original and replication study/reference but a different ratio. When assigning entries to FReD Data Curators, entries with overlapping studies are typically assigned to the same FReD Data Curator pair.            |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Study  | A study is an empirical investigation made in one of the reports. One entry usually consists of exactly two references/reports. Each of the references/reports can consist of multiple studies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Row    | One row in the database consists of one pair of original and replication effects that correspond to a claim made in the original study. In other words, one row is one pair of *findings*.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Claim  | Each row must contain a claim that was made in the original report and that is tested again in the replication report. Multiple rows from one entry can have the same claim (e.g., a claim is tested using multiple statistical tests). Specific differences between identical claims are noted in a *description* variable.                                                                                                                                          |
+--------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```{r status, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
    na_if("na.pdf") %>%
```

```{r add-clean-refs, include = FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# Load shared citation caching functions
source("../crossref_citation_cache.R")

# Get unique DOIs from both original and replication studies
dois_o <- ds %>% 
  filter(!is.na(doi_o)) %>% 
  distinct(doi_o) %>% 
  pull(doi_o)

dois_r <- ds %>% 
  filter(!is.na(doi_r)) %>% 
  distinct(doi_r) %>% 
  pull(doi_r)

# Fetch references using shared cache
refs_o <- get_apa_references(dois_o)
refs_r <- get_apa_references(dois_r)

# Join references to dataset
ds <- ds %>% 
  mutate(doi_r = tolower(doi_r),
         doi_o = tolower(doi_o)) %>% 
  left_join(
    refs_o %>% rename(doi_o = doi, ref_o_new = reference)
  ) %>% left_join(
    refs_r %>% rename(doi_r = doi, ref_r_new = reference)
  ) %>% 
  mutate(ref_o = coalesce(ref_o_new, ref_o),
         ref_r = coalesce(ref_r_new, ref_r)) %>% 
  select(-ref_o_new, -ref_r_new)

```

### Computation of Standardized Effect Sizes

Original studies and replications report effect sizes in a wide range of metrics. Where meaningful, we provide the reported values alongside a conversion to *r* (Pearson's correlation coefficient), using the [function in the FReD R package](https://forrt.org/FReD/reference/convert_effect_sizes.html). However, this is not always possible or meaningful, particularly where effect sizes do not express an unconditional bivariate relationship (e.g., interaction effects or partial correlations), and where they do not encode the direction of an effect (e.g., R² or F-statistics). In these cases, the quantitative replication results will not show whether the pattern matches (e.g., two F test could be significant due to opposite interaction patterns). The table below shows how we have proceeded in this dataset.

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Action                                                                                                                          | Effect Size Types                                                                                                                              |
+=================================================================================================================================+================================================================================================================================================+
| Used as correlation                                                                                                             | r, Phi                                                                                                                                         |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Converted to correlation                                                                                                        | Odds Ratio, Cohen's d, Hedges's g, test statistics (t test), Z values                                                                          |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Did not convert, but provide [function](https://forrt.org/FReD/reference/convert_effect_sizes.html) if analysts wish to convert | R², Eta squared, test statistics (F with df1 = 1 and χ² test), Cohen's f, Cohen's f², partial Eta squared                                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| No conversion                                                                                                                   | test statistics (F with df1 \> 1, proportion test, binomial test), partial correlation, Cohen's dz, Cramer's V, Omega, regression coefficients |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```{r effectsize conversion, include = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE) 

# convert original effect sizes
ds$r_o <- convert_effect_sizes(es_values = ds$es_value_o, es_types = ds$es_type_o)  

# convert replication effect sizes
ds$r_r <- convert_effect_sizes(es_values = ds$es_value_r, es_types = ds$es_type_r)
```

## Replication success

Replication success can be defined in different ways. Here, we provide two variables - one that is based on the authors' subjective interpretation of the replication results *at the study/entry level* and one that is based on a statistical criterion at the level of *individual claims*.

### Author's reported success variable

We reviewed the reports to identify how authors interpreted their results. This is coded based on the abstract where possible, and the conclusion/discussion/results section otherwise. The variable `reported_success` is coded as follows:

-   `success` when the authors interpret their replication as successful (e.g., "we successfully replicated...")
-   `failure` when the authors interpret their replication as unsuccessful (e.g., "we failed to replicate...")
-   `mixed` when the authors describe their results as mixed or as a partial replication

There are a few more specific categories that are used less frequently:

-   `uninformative` when the authors explicitly describe their results as uninformative, e.g. due to a small sample size
-   `statistically successful but flawed` when the authors replicate the original finding but *primarily* do so to show that the method is flawed, and that an alternative analysis yields different results
-   `descriptive only` when authors describe patterns but do not draw comparative conclusions.

The variables `reported_success_quote` and `reported_success_quote_source` provide the quote (or decision rule) that was used to code the variable and the section of the report where it was found.

```{r add-subjective-success, include = TRUE, echo = FALSE}

  mutate(doi_o = tolower(doi_o),

  filter(!is.na(outcome), validation != "validated - discarded") %>% 
  group_by(doi_o, id_r, study_o, study_r) %>%
  arrange(desc(validation == "validated - chosen")) %>% 
  slice_head(n = 1) %>% 
  ungroup()

reported_success <- reported_success %>% 
  select(doi_o, id_r, study_o, study_r, 
                              reported_success = outcome,
                              reported_success_quote = outcome_quote,
                              reported_success_quote_source = out_quote_source) 
# Check for missing entries

ds <- ds %>% left_join(reported_success, by = c("doi_o", "id_r", "study_o", "study_r"))

p_data <- ds %>%

    reported_success, 
    levels = rev(c("successful", "mixed", "failed", "uninformative",

  )) %>%

         frequency = paste0(round(pct, 1), " % (", n, ")"))

 #p_data %>% mutate(label = paste0(reported_success, ": ", label)) %>% pull(label) %>% clipr::write_clip()
```

### Statistical success variable

There are many different statistical indicators of replication success (many of which can be calculated with the [FReD package](https://forrt.org/FReD/articles/success_criteria.html)). However, for this project COS defines success as a significant result *in the same direction* as the original finding.

This is not trivial to derive from the data where effect sizes are not directional. We provide a `statistical_success` variable that is defined as follows:

-   `TRUE` when the replication is significant (based on the reported p-value, at alpha = .05) and the reported effect size is directional and in the same direction as the original. Note that this includes cases where effect sizes cannot be converted into a common metric, such as regression coefficients.

-   `FALSE` when the replication is not significant, or the reported effect size is directional and in the opposite direction as the original.

-   `NA` when the replication effect size is not directional (e.g, Eta squared, F-tests, R²) or when the original study was not significant (or did not report an effect size, so that the direction cannot be obtained programmatically).

<details>

<summary>Click here for a list of directional and non-directional effect size types</summary>

-   *Directional:* odds ratios, correlations (r and phi), Cohen's d / Hedges' g, t-test, Z, regression weights (b, beta), mean difference

-   *Non-directional:* η² (and partial), F-test, R²

</details>

```{r success, include = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.show = TRUE)

# directional effects
dir_types <- c("d", "r", "OR", "phi", "b (unstd)", "beta (std)", "beta", 
               "Mean difference", "percentage difference", "hedges' g",
               "median difference")

ds <- ds %>% 
  mutate(es_type_o = str_trim(es_type_o),
         es_type_r = str_trim(es_type_r))

ds <- ds %>% mutate(
  p_val_temp_r = coalesce(as.numeric(pval_value_r), FReD:::p_from_r(r_r, as.numeric(n_r))),
   p_val_temp_o = coalesce(as.numeric(pval_value_o), FReD:::p_from_r(r_o, as.numeric(n_o))),
  convertible_o = 
    es_type_o %in% dir_types | str_detect(es_value_o, "^t|^Z|^z"),
  convertible_r = es_type_r %in% dir_types | str_detect(es_value_r, "^t|^Z|^z"),
  convertible = convertible_o & convertible_r,
  statistical_success = case_when(
    !convertible |  p_val_temp_o > .05 | 
      (p_val_temp_o == .05 & pval_type_o == "g (>)") | is.na(es_value_o) |
      is.na(es_value_r) | is.na(p_val_temp_r) | is.na(p_val_temp_o) ~ NA,
    (p_val_temp_r < .05 | (p_val_temp_r == .05 & pval_type_r == "l (<)")) & 
    sign(if_else(!is.na(r_r), r_r, as.numeric(es_value_r))) == 
    sign(if_else(!is.na(r_o), r_o, as.numeric(es_value_o))) ~ TRUE,
    .default = FALSE
  ),
  r_o = if_else(convertible_o, r_o, NA_real_),
  r_r = if_else(convertible_r, r_r, NA_real_)) %>% 
  select(-convertible, p_val_temp_r, p_val_temp_o)
```

Out of `r nrow(ds)` rows, `statistical_success` could be calculated for `r sum(!is.na(ds$statistical_success))` rows. Among these, `r round(mean(ds$statistical_success, na.rm = TRUE)*100, 1)`% were statistically successful (significant in the same direction) and `r round(mean(!ds$statistical_success, na.rm = TRUE)*100, 1)`% could be considered failures.

```{r scatterplot, echo = FALSE}
df_temp <- ds
df_temp$statistical_success <- as.character(df_temp$statistical_success)
df_temp$statistical_success[is.na(df_temp$statistical_success)] <- "uncertain"
df_temp$statistical_success[df_temp$statistical_success == "TRUE"] <- "yes"
df_temp$statistical_success[df_temp$statistical_success == "FALSE"] <- "no"

scatterplot <-
  ggplot(df_temp, aes(x = r_o, y = r_r, text = description)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = statistical_success)) +
    scale_color_manual(
      name = "Replication Success",
      values = c("yes" = "#2ECC40", "no" = "#FF4136", "uncertain" = "grey50"),
      breaks = c("yes", "no", "uncertain"),
      labels = c("yes" = "Yes", "no" = "No", "uncertain" = "Uncertain")
    ) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = 2) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "Grey60") +
    scale_x_continuous(name = "Original Effect Size", limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Replication Effect Size", limits = c(-.5, 1), breaks = c(-.5, -.25, 0, .25, .5, .75, 1)) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(caption = "Coded at the row/claim level. Only includes directional effect sizes that could be converted to *r*")
    
    plotly::ggplotly(scatterplot, tooltip = "text") %>%
      plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE) %>%
      plotly::layout(xaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE), yaxis = list(fixedrange = TRUE))
```

## Codebook

The finalized dataset includes the variables that COS and FORRT agreed on as well as further variables that FORRT found necessary to understand the entered value. More detailed datasets are available upon request. A synthesis of the current version of the FORRT Replication Database with the new data format is planned for fall 2025.

NB: Beware that the `entry_id` and `effect_id` variables are *not* stable across versions of the dataset. They are re-generated for each version of the dataset to ensure that entries and effects are numbered consecutively. If you want to identify entries uniquely across versions of the data, it is better to rely on a combination of `doi_o`, `study_o`, `doi_r` (and `url_r`), and `study_r`.

```{r codebook, echo = FALSE}

codebook <- openxlsx::read.xlsx("cos_codebook.xlsx")

DT::datatable(codebook, extensions = 'FixedColumns', options = list(pageLength = 300, dom = 't', rownames = FALSE, scroller = FALSE), rownames = FALSE)

```

## Validated Dataset

```{r final dataset, echo = FALSE}

# number entries and effects

ds <- ds %>% 
  mutate(entry = paste(doi_o, study_o, id_r, study_r),
         entry_id = match(entry, unique(entry))) %>%
  group_by(entry) %>%
  mutate(effect_id = row_number()) %>% 
  ungroup()

ds_final <- ds %>% select(all_of(codebook$Variable))

openxlsx::write.xlsx(ds_final, file = paste(Sys.Date(), "_COSdata_validated.xlsx", sep = ""))

list_of_studies <- ds_final[, c("ref_o", "ref_r", "discipline")]
list_of_studies <- list_of_studies[!duplicated(list_of_studies), ]
list_of_studies <- list_of_studies[order(list_of_studies$ref_o), ] # sort by original study
list_of_studies <- list_of_studies[order(list_of_studies$ref_r), ] # sort by replication study

```

## Some warnings and caveats

-   **Study numbers**: Please note that for large scale replication projects, there are no consistently reported study numbers. In this dataset, we use study numbers to consistently identify them but not necessarily to reflect the study order in the replication article or the associated dataset.

-   **Pre-Prints**: It is possible that some replication studies that are coded as preprints have been published in a journal in the meantime.

-   **Eta-squared**: Our [conversion function](https://forrt.org/FReD/reference/convert_effect_sizes.html) converts eta-squared but not partial eta-squared. It is possible that authors misreported one as the other.

-   **`entry_id` and `effect_id` variables are *not* stable across versions of the dataset**. They should thus not be used to identify entries over time. They are re-generated for each version of the dataset to ensure that entries and effects are numbered consecutively. If you want to identify entries uniquely across versions of the data, it is better to rely on a combination of `doi_o`, `study_o`, `doi_r` (and `url_r`), and `study_r`.

-   **Selection of rows:** A statistical result in a replication can be assigned to two different original results from the same paper (e.g., when the original only reported separate effects for sub-samples but replication focused on total sample), and an original result can be combined with multiple replication results. Also, matched effects are not comprehensive but selected by the coders for being linked to the relevant claim. Therefore, rows should not be treated as independent.

## Internal Process

Entries were initially drawn from the [FORRT Replication Database](https://forrt-replications.shinyapps.io/fred_explorer/), which consists of crowdsourced data that has been single-coded and partially validated, an unsystematic list of additional replications we have maintained, and a broad literature search. A snapshot description of the FORRT Replication Database from October 2023 was published [here](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.101). Given that psychology has conducted the largest replication projets to date, the dataset is biased towards psychology, but we aimed to include other fields where possible.

Each entry is assigned to two FReD Data Curators, who independently complete all variables. They are collected by the FReD-team in a Google Spreadsheet for validation and run through a [cleaning-script](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forrtproject/FReD-data/refs/heads/main/clean_cos_fred.R). Most of the time, the values from one Data Curator are revised and chosen and the others are superseded. It is possible to choose a combination or all of the rows of an entry if different effects were coded by the FReD Data Curators.
